sections.subtitle: EPRA measures strip out non-cash revaluations and are the REIT industry's preferred underlying-earnings basis

epraEarnings.title: EPRA earnings and EPRA EPS
epraEarnings.content:
EPRA earnings is the European REIT industry's standard measure of recurring underlying profit: statutory net income with revaluation movements, gains/losses on disposals and other non-cash or one-off items stripped out. EPRA EPS divides it by the share count.

For Hammerson: statutory NetIncome swings from large non-cash revaluations (FY2019-2021 wrote the portfolio down heavily; FY2025 wrote it back up), while EPRA earnings is the steadier number management and analysts use to set the dividend. Compare this chart with Net Income vs FCF to see how much of the reported swing is revaluation noise.

What to watch:

  • EPRA EPS trend versus the dividend per share -- the payout is set against this, not statutory EPS
  • The two placings in Aug-25 and Aug-26 diluted the share count, so EPRA EPS growth is slower than EPRA earnings growth

leverage.title: LTV and Net Debt / EBITDA
leverage.content:
LTV (loan-to-value) is net debt divided by the portfolio's valuation -- the REIT's core covenant and solvency metric. Net Debt / EBITDA is the same leverage measured against annual cash earnings rather than asset value.

For Hammerson: LTV rose back to ~38-39% in FY2025/H1 FY2026 (from a FY2024 low of 30%) as the Value Retail and Italian outlet acquisitions were funded partly with debt; the DCF values the equity directly from EPRA-style earnings at the cost of equity and deliberately holds net debt at zero in the engine (see the DCF notes below) precisely because this leverage is already embedded in the finance costs that earnings is stated after.

What to watch:

  • LTV against Hammerson's own ~40% ceiling and banking covenants
  • Net Debt/EBITDA falling as NRI from acquisitions comes through a full year, versus rising if further acquisitions are debt-funded

interestCover.title: Interest cover
interestCover.content:
Interest cover is EBITDA (or EPRA earnings before interest) divided by net finance costs -- how many times over the REIT can pay its interest bill from operating earnings.

For Hammerson: cover fell to 2.3x in FY2021 when NRI was depressed by COVID rent concessions and the portfolio was more indebted; it has since more than doubled to ~5x as NRI recovered and debt was paid down, which is the deleveraging story behind the LTV chart above.

What to watch:

  • Cover trending back down if the recent acquisitions' debt costs outpace their NRI contribution
  • Covenant headroom disclosed in the annual report (typically a minimum cover ratio)

netRentalIncome.title: Net rental income vs revenue
netRentalIncome.content:
Net rental income (NRI) is rental income after direct property costs (service charge shortfalls, void rates, estate management) -- the REIT's true operating revenue line, as distinct from the Revenue column which may include gross rents and service-charge pass-throughs before those costs are netted off.

For Hammerson: the DCF's base revenue is NRI, not the Revenue column, because NRI is proportionally consolidated across joint ventures (e.g. Value Retail, VIA Outlets) and is the figure management guides to. NRI fell from £182.5m (FY2021) to £146.0m (FY2024) as Hammerson disposed of retail parks and non-core assets, then rebounded to £180.2m in FY2025 as the Value Retail and outlet acquisitions added NRI back.

What to watch:

  • NRI growth from like-for-like occupancy/rent versus from acquisitions
  • The gap between NRI and Revenue, which marks costs the landlord cannot recover from tenants

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Hammerson plc: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Hammerson plc: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Hammerson plc: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Hammerson plc: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Hammerson plc: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

nta.title: NTA per share
nta.content:
NTA per share is net tangible assets divided by shares -- the book value of the portfolio.

For Hammerson plc: the share price relative to NTA is the market's view of the portfolio's valuation and management.

What to watch:

  • Discount or premium to NTA
  • NTA growth from revaluations versus retained cash

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Hammerson plc: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Hammerson plc: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Hammerson plc: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Hammerson plc: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
